title_en: Anthropic’s historic stock market debut: key takeaways, and what comes next for the AI industry
excerpt_en: A record breaking IPO has raised billions for the AI frontier lab – but experts say the coming months could prove bumpy, as the industry faces a variety of challenges
body_en: In the end, Anthropic’s much-anticipated IPO more than lived up to the hype. The market’s embrace of one of the AI industry’s most talked about companies has resulted in the maker of the Claude chatbot becoming one of the world’s most valuable firms after just one day of trading.

With many of the company’s founders, investors and employees now worth billions of dollars – and demand for the company’s stock remaining resilient – attention now turns to the stability of the wider market, and the global headwinds that experts say could threaten the AI industry over the coming months.
Here’s a rundown of what we can gather after a big day for Anthropic and the AI industry

Biggest IPO in history, but it’s not all good news Closing the day about 17% higher than its initial public offering price, Anthropic shares were trading at just over $97 when the market closed taking its valuation to roughly $1.7tn. The share price initially soared by 34% when trading got under way on Thursday, briefly taking the company’s valuation to more than $2tn.
The blockbuster debut easily places the IPO as the biggest in history, with the 980m shares sold raising $81bn, surpassing the previous record held by Elon Musk’s SpaceX’s $75bn raised in June.
Despite the excitement, major US stock indexes fells to seven-month lows on Thursday, dragged down by growing concerns about the longer-term outlook for the AI industry.

“The blockbuster Anthropic launch is a critical step in reassuring the market about the potential for AI, but it’s really just the beginning,” said Bob O’Donnell, chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research.

We still need to see ‌what happens with OpenAI, how the Nvidia situation evolves, how ‌the political climate for data centres shapes up, and what the historical performance for Anthropic proves to be before we’ll get any real sense of stability.”
In early trading on Friday, Asian stocks plunged by up to 4%, suggesting Anthropic’s debut has done little to settle nerves on trading floors.
A staggering rise in revenue... and debt According to reports demand for Anthropic shares was about six times what the company was able to offer, an incredible result for a company founded in 2021.

Started by a number of former OpenAI employees, Anthropic initially lagged behind its rival frontier lab, but analysts say its focus on building software for business and programming clients has helped to position it as one of the market leaders.
That breakneck growth has left investors stunned; from fledgling start-up six years ago, Anthropic is now worth more than US stock market stalwarts Walmart, JP Morgan, Visa and ExxonMobil.
The speed of its growth is reflected in its revenue: according to its investor prospectus, Anthropic brought in $16.2bn in the first six months of 2026, up from $4.6bn in revenue for all of 2025.

But Anthropic has also lost an enormous amount of money. In the first half of 2026, the company reported losses of $80bn, though that was largely due to a one-off charge. Losses grew to $104bn in the first nine months of 2026. The firm has said its costs will balloon as it invests further in datacentres.

The IPO hands Anthropic a pool of new cash to make those investments, but with promises to spend about $900bn on datacentre infrastructure over the next two decades, experts say their debt is likely to rise even further.
We need to talk about datacentres Newly minted Anthropic investors will also have to contend with rising public sentiment against AI.

Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei has been among the loudest voices pointing out the dangers that the products he and his rivals are developing may pose to humanity. He has called for a slowdown on the development of the most advanced AI models after employees expressed concerns that they were being built irresponsibly.

Across the US, opposition to AI companies has manifested in protests against local datacentre plans, with a number of municipalities and states voting for bans or restrictions on them at the recent midterm elections.

US economic growth is inextricably tied to the booming AI sector, and in particular the vast investments in datacentres that power programmes like Claude and ChatGPT. One estimate from Harvard professor Jason Furman suggested “investment in information processing equipment and software” accounted for 92% of the US’s GDP growth in the first half of 2025.
Any slowdown in that expenditure on datacentres could therefore have far-reaching consequences for Anthropic – and the global economy.

Democrats eye a crackdown Anthropic’s leaders are also likely looking ahead to the changes to government next year, when Democrats take over both chambers of Congress after securing large majorities in the midterm elections.

Senior Democrats have already suggested that tech companies could face a regulatory crackdown over the dangers that advanced AI models pose, and over the volatility that AI IPOs could introduce into the economy.

title_en: ‘The Pacific is not for sale’: outcry after US holds first deep sea mining lease sale near American Samoa
excerpt_en: Multi-million dollar sale comes despite a federal judge in Hawaii voiding the environmental clearance it had been given to proceed
body_en: The US has carried out its first ever deep-sea mining lease sales off the coast of American Samoa, despite an adverse court ruling earlier this week and mounting local opposition.

The sales took place on Thursday in a live-streamed auction of 12.7m hectares (31.5m acres) of seabed off the US territory’s coast marked for mineral exploration. Two areas of the Pacific archipelago were sold for $3m each to Wetstone US Ventures, the only bidder, according to a spokesperson for the Marine Minerals Administration (MMA).

The buyers gain permission to conduct preliminary activities such as carry out bathymetric and geophysical mapping, among other data. The golf ball-sized metallic nodules that miners are searching for are touted as a source of rare earths and minerals needed for technologies, such as electric vehicles, renewable energy and defence systems.

“This is the first time the United States has held an offshore critical minerals lease sale in the Pacific and a historic step for America’s energy and mineral security,” said interior secretary Doug Burgum in a statement.
Related: US territories hit out at Trump plan to explore deep sea mining in the Pacific

In his opening remarks at the California auction, Mike Olsen, director of the MMA, said the federal action today aligns with the Trump administration’s agenda “to advance the responsible development of America’s offshore critical mineral resources.”
“As we look to America’s next 250 years, we want future generations to inherit a nation that can build and innovate here at home, on the lands and in the waters that we’ve stewarded,” Olsen said.

However, the move comes despite a federal judge this week in Hawaii voiding the environmental clearance it had been given to proceed, ruling that the Endangered Species Act (ESA) had been violated. Judge Jill Otake wrote: “NMFS [National Marine Fisheries Service] failed to even attempt to consider the potential effects on ESA-listed species.”

Earthjustice, which filed the petition, said the ruling made Thursday’s auction unlawful. “We will use the full extent of the law to vigorously push for the leases to be voided,” Earthjustice attorney Chris Eaton said in a statement.

Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka, founder of Finafinau, an American Samoan youth and environment nonprofit, said: “More than 76,000 public comments, repeated calls for meaningful consultation, and now a federal court ruling that the government violated the Endangered Species Act. Yet here we are, watching our ocean being auctioned to the highest bidder.”

On the eve of the auction, Finafinau filed a fresh petition seeking an injunction with the district court of Hawaii in an unsuccessful last-minute bid to stop the lease sale. The lawsuit slammed the Trump administration for barrelling toward the sale “without sufficient information to comprehensively evaluate the impacts of issuing the first-ever commercial deep-sea mining leases”.

Taryn Kiekow Heimer, director of Ocean Energy at the non-profit Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), warned that the American Samoa sale would now become the template for subsequent applications from mining companies.

“These leases last at least 20 years. The Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam are next in line,” Heimer said. “If this goes through, the administration will have shown it can open the deep sea over the objections of the people who live closest to it.”

A second lease sale involving 27.9m hectares (69m acres) of seabed between the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam is tentatively scheduled for 16 December. It is locked in a similar lawsuit that is pending in the federal court of Hawaii.

Guam Senator William Parkinson called on the US government to cancel the auction. “You don’t get to sell off our ocean first and ask whether it’s legal later. Washington needs to understand that the Pacific is not for sale,” he told the Guardian.
He said this week’s federal court decision “exposes the arrogance and recklessness of an administration that treats our ocean as a corporate commodity and Pacific Islanders as expendable.”
American Samoa governor, Pulaali’i Nikolao Pula, has previously said the deep sea mining auctions could “unlock scientiﬁc knowledge” and “create economic opportunities” for the territory.
John Wasko, an advocate of deep-sea mining, said the emerging industry, which is touted as supporting the electric vehicle sector, was the answer to climate change.

“Everybody wants unlimited renewable energy. Nobody wants to admit their part in planet Earth’s atmospheric destruction,” said Wasko, executive director of American Samoa Development Council, a non-profit group that endorses deep-sea mining in American Samoa.

The legal battle continues. In this week’s lawsuit, Finafinau asked the court to nullify the lease sale. “Despite venturing into largely uncharted territory, MMA recklessly accelerated environmental review,” its court filing states. “With this lease sale, the federal government has rushed to open the ocean floor to commercial mining for the first time, despite its limited understanding of the significant environmental consequences.”

title_en: Xi-Putin-Trump summit was heavy on symbolism, light on substance – and not exactly a Yalta II
excerpt_en: At an eagerly anticipated summit, the leaders of China, Russia and US discussed nuclear weapons – but not much else.
body_en: China's Xi Jinping places himself firmly in the center of the trilateral summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump. Doug Mills/Getty Images It was touted as a history-making summit of the year. Presidents Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping sat down on Nov. 19, 2026, in Shenzhen, China, on the sideline of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, for the first such trilateral meeting of the three leaders.
Going into the talks, the trio had much to dicuss: the ongoing war in Ukraine, Middle East conflict and the march of artificial intelligence technology chief among them.
But what did 90 minutes of conversation deliver?
As an expert on U.S.-China relations at Harvard Kennedy School, I saw a lot of style, but less substance.

At an eagerly anticipated summit, the leaders of China, Russia and US discussed nuclear weapons – but not much else. What were the key takeaways from the meeting? The first thing to pay attention to is the symbolism of the occasion. And so much of what was presented in Shenzhen was about the body language of the three men, their interactions and what that may indicate in regards to how they view themselves in a potentially new global order.

And this was on show even before the leaders sat down. At the beginning of the trip, when Trump landed in Shenzhen, he was met by Xi. Meeting a foreign leader at the airport is seen as a special honor bestowed by the Chinese president.
And then came a hug – that really was unprecedented. I haven’t seen the general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party hug anyone before – certainly not his Politburo comrades.

A rare airport hug from Xi Jinping. Mandel Ngan/Getty Images It was all choreographed, of course. But it continued into the summit itself. The picture of a big table with Trump, Putin and Xi there is also symbolic. And look who was in the middle: Xi. Here we have China presenting as the “Middle Kingdom,” steadying the world. Whether that is an accurate depiction of China’s global presence is beside the point – it is how Xi would like Beijing to be seen.
In terms of policy, however, not much was actually done, but we did get a glimpse of what was on the three leaders’ minds.

So we had talk of reforming the U.N. – something all three agree needs to be done. In particular, China wants more power in the organization, while Trump has become increasingly disillusioned with the international body.

And there was also a lot of discussion on nuclear weapons controls. In fact, all three signed off on a document that made statements and aspirations – with fewer commitments – to tamping down nuclear threats. Interestingly, this was all based around a phrase that U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev first aired in 1985: “Nuclear war cannot be won, must never be fought.”

All three leaders signed onto the phrase, although there was not an awful lot of substance on how nuclear controls would be implemented. The main treaties on the matter expired a while ago, and Beijing, which lags behind Washington and Moscow in regards to capacity, may have different thoughts on the matter.

President Donald Trump shakes hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China’s President Xi Jinping looks on in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 18, 2026. Iori Sagisawa/AFP via Getty Images What wasn’t discussed? The big thing not discussed in any substantive way was the wars raging in the domains of two of the three nations.

For Trump, that means Iran. Washington has not been able to bring the conflict in Iran to a conclusion some nine months after it began. The thinking going into the summit may have been that if China – or even Russia – were able to help pressure Iran and bring an end to the conflict, that would be encouraged.

But the spectacle of the U.S. not being able to end the war in Iran is not, I suspect, something that the Russians and Chinese are in a rush to bring to an end. In any case, neither appeared willing to give up a key card – assistance to Washington in the matter – in this meeting.

At the other end of that Eurasian spectrum is Ukraine. It was not mentioned by name at the summit. Besides the fact that the three leaders are not on the same side of the conflict, there is also the fact that Ukraine’s European allies were not in the room – and it would have been far too much for Europe for Trump to make news on Ukraine in the company of Putin and Xi.

Beyond those conflicts, AI regulation and critical mineral supply chains were not discussed by the three leaders. But that isn’t to say that those issues – crucial ones in the U.S.-China economic rivalry – were not brought up in the bilateral conversations that took place in Shenzhen. It may be that they were heard in these more discreet, private settings.

British Prime Minister Winston Churchill, U.S. President Franklin Roosevelt and Soviet Premier Joseph Stalin sit together at the Yalta Conference. AP Photo This was touted as Yalta II – was it? There were some immediate similarities with the Yalta Conference – the February 1945 summit at which the U.K.’s Winston Churchill, Joseph Stalin of the Soviet Union and U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt planned out the end of World War II and began discussing postwar Europe. But these were largely about the imagery of the three men around the table.

title_en: Myanmar genocide ruling is a watershed moment in international justice – with huge ramifications for other cases
excerpt_en: The International Court of Justice’s historic finding against the leaders who directed attacks against the Rohingya may affect other cases, including against Israel.
body_en: International Court of Justice President Iwasawa Yuji reads the court's judgment in The Hague on Nov. 19, 2026. Jeroen Jumelet/ANP/AFP via Getty Images The International Court of Justice’s historic ruling of genocide against Myanmar on Nov. 19, 2026, will have significant consequences for the parties involved in the case – and potentially some who are not.

The Hague’s highly anticipated judgment in Gambia v. Myanmar is a major victory for Gambia, the tiny west African nation that filed a complaint with the court against Myanmar in 2019. It is also a major moment of accountability for the military leadership of Myanmar.

But as an expert in genocide and mass atrocity prevention, I believe the ruling goes far beyond these nations. Indeed, it is also a watershed moment for international legal justice that is bound to have important effects on the court’s other ongoing genocide cases, particularly the case of South Africa v. Israel.

Rohingya refugees watch the International Court of Justice ruling on a screen at a camp in Bangladesh’s Cox’s Bazar on Nov. 19, 2026. Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP via Getty Images What the court ruled Gambia’s case focused on actions that Myanmar’s military government called “clearance operations” in the course of its decades-long violent persecution of the country’s Muslim Rohingya minority.

The Tatmadaw, as the Myanmar military is known, justified these actions as a counterinsurgency operation. Yet in the course of those attacks, soldiers were found to have destroyed hundreds of Rohingya villages, and to have committed widespread rapes, torture and summary killings.

While the precise death toll of the 2017 attacks may never be known, at least 10,000 Rohingya civilians are thought to have died, and roughly 750,000 Rohingya fled to neighboring Bangladesh. There they joined other Rohingya in what is now the world’s largest refugee camp of over 1.2 million people, comprised of those who had already fled years of the Myanmar government’s persecution and attacks.

The court’s ruling that the Tatmadaw’s attacks amounted to genocide rested on its interpretation of the crime of genocide in the 1948 U.N. Genocide Convention, the first major international treaty approved by the United Nations General Assembly.

For an attack to be genocidal, it must be directed against an ethnic, religious, racial or national group, and must include at least one of five prohibited acts: killing members of a group; inflicting serious physical or mental harm on members; deliberately inflicting conditions calculated to bring about its destruction; imposing measures intended to prevent births; or forcibly transferring children from the group.
Beyond these factual requirements, genocide requires that the perpetrator specifically intended these acts to destroy the group, in whole or in part.

In its ruling, the court agreed that the facts of Myanmar’s attacks met the legal definition of genocide. For the notoriously difficult and demanding requirement for proving the “ special intent ” to destroy a group, the court determined that the pattern, selective targeting and lethality of the attacks on Rohingya villages could not plausibly be explained as a counterinsurgency operation.
Instead, the only reasonable inference that could be drawn from the military’s actions, the court determined, was the specific intent to destroy the Rohingya ethnic minority.
A series of historic firsts The court’s decision is unprecedented in many important respects.

In an influential previous ruling on violations of the Genocide Convention, in Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro in 2007, the court found only that Serbia had not met its legal duty to prevent genocide by failing to use its influence to restrain the Bosnian Serb army in the Srebrenica massacre of 1995.
In the Myanmar ruling, by contrast, the court ruled for the first time that a country is legally responsible for committing genocide – not merely failing to prevent it.

Further, the court ruled for the first time that a country that has committed genocide also has multiple obligations toward the victim group. Those include designing and implementing a comprehensive program of reparations and compensation for victims; creating conditions where Rohingya can make a safe, voluntary and dignified return to their homes; and restoration of their citizenship status after national legislation from 1982 rendered them stateless.

Rohingya Refugees cross a river at Tambru, a no-man’s land on the Bangladesh-Myanmar border. Majority World/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Finally, the court also demanded that Myanmar take steps to investigate all those involved in the genocide to determine individual criminal responsibility. Since the International Court of Justice is not a criminal court and only hears cases between states, this order explicitly connects the ruling to other courts where individual perpetrators can be held accountable.

These include the International Criminal Court – which had already requested an arrest warrant for Tatmadaw leader Min Aung Hlaing – as well as national courts that may pursue prosecution according to the doctrine of universal jurisdiction.
The ruling’s broader implications The court’s ruling in Gambia vs. Myanmar is also likely to have huge ramifications far beyond the case itself.

In filing its complaint, Gambia appealed to an innovative argument to establish that it had legal standing. It argued for what’s known as “ erga omnes partes,” roughly translated as “toward all parties to a treaty.” According to this line of reasoning, the Genocide Convention imposes such strong legal duties to prevent and punish the crime of genocide that any state, even one that has not in any way been directly harmed, has the standing – in fact, the obligation – to seek legal remedies.

title_en: US warned supplying nuclear-powered submarines to Australia would diminish its own fleet for ‘many years’
excerpt_en: Congressional Budget Office also questions whether Australian-flagged vessels could be compelled into a conflict with China under Aukus deal
body_en: Providing nuclear-powered submarines to Australia would diminish the US navy’s own fleet for “many years”, a new report for the US Congress has cautioned, questioning whether Australian-flagged vessels could be compelled into service in a conflict with China.

The US navy’s latest shipbuilding plan does not countenance the Aukus agreement in its forecasts at all, noting only in a footnote that the transfer of any Virginia-class submarine to Australia “has not been factored into the plan”, the report says.

But the Congressional Budget Office has evaluated the impact of Aukus, releasing detailed analysis on Friday morning, finding “the US submarine industrial base is currently struggling to meet the Navy’s demand for submarines”.
“Increasing production further to replace SSNs [attack submarines] sold to Australia would increase the challenges that the Navy and the shipyards are facing,” the report found.
“The sale of SSNs to Australia would reduce the number of attack submarines available to the Navy for many years.”
Related: Aukus is ‘worst, riskiest and most costly’ Australian defence decision ever, public inquiry into submarine deal says
Under the so-called “Pillar One” of Aukus, the US has agreed to sell between three and five in-service Virginia-class submarines to Australia, beginning in 2032.
The CBO analysis questioned whether any submarines transferred to Australia could be utilised in the event of a US conflict with China.
“Would China be less deterred if the United States reduced the number of its attack submarines to help Australia develop its own submarine force?”

The report argued that because of the longstanding, and robust, alliance between the US and Australia, boosting the Australian navy’s submarine fleet could help offset the US Navy’s “potential loss of capability”.

“That loss might even be more than offset because the Australian submarines would be based in the Western Pacific region and therefore could respond more quickly to any conflict with China over Taiwan or other issues in the South China Sea.
“However, Australia would control its own submarines, and their participation in any particular conflict would not be guaranteed.”

In 2023, Australia’s defence minister, Richard Marles, said Australia would make no promises it would deploy its submarines in support of any US conflict with China, and that any future Australian submarines would be “under the complete control of the Australian government of the day”.

Submarine-building rates in the US have been tenaciously laggard. The country’s shipyards are currently producing Virginia-class submarines at a rate of 1.13 a year: that rate needs to lift that to two submarines a year to service America’s own needs, and 2.33 a year to have additional boats to transfer to Australia.
The CBO report said submarine-building rates had slowed over the past two decades, and Virginia-class submarines were delayed between 24 and 36 months.
“Building … submarines took five to six years in the 2000s but now takes an average of 10 to 11 years, according to current schedules.”

The US legislation governing Aukus states that the president of the US can only transfer a submarine to Australia if losing that submarine from US service “ will not degrade the United States undersea capabilities”.
The US can refuse to transfer any submarines to Australia without penalty, under the terms of the Aukus agreement.
Related: Gender-diverse Australian sailors barred from US submarines despite Aukus deal, documents reveal
Critics of Aukus have said there is vanishingly little chance the US will have the capacity to sell any of its in-service submarines to Australia.

The former foreign affairs minister Bob Carr told Guardian Australia both countries were “living a lie” in upholding the fiction that the submarine deal would happen. “It’s now conventional wisdom in Washington as well as in Canberra that we’re not going to get the subs.”

But the deal has avowed, bipartisan broad political support across both the US and Australia. Marles said earlier this month: “ Aukus is happening, our alliance is happening, and all of that continues unimpeded.”

title_en: The U.S. Paid Insurers Billions to Cover Civilians Harmed in War. Even the Government Says the System Is Ripe for Fraud.
excerpt_en: The post The U.S. Paid Insurers Billions to Cover Civilians Harmed in War. Even the Government Says the System Is Ripe for Fraud. appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: It was supposed to be a safety net for the workers who helped the United States fight its wars — a federal program that provided healthcare and financial support to the employees of government contractors injured or killed in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Instead, a handful of America’s insurance companies have become its biggest beneficiaries. While reaping billions in government payments, they have delayed care for legitimate injuries and received reimbursements for fraudulent claims, a ProPublica investigation found.

Over the past decade, American taxpayers have paid nearly $5 billion to insurers through the obscure program, which the government itself has described as “ripe for potential fraud or, at the very least, gamesmanship for profit,” according to an internal memo ProPublica obtained.

Nobody knows the true amount of misspent money. The official who oversaw the program under the Biden administration estimated that between $100 to $150 million is being wasted annually. The money has poured from a forgotten system for forgotten people who suffered forgotten injuries and deaths in America’s wars.
It would be difficult to find another federal program with more incentives for graft and fewer controls to prevent it, the investigation found.

The Labor Department has proven incapable of policing the program. No standards exist to determine whether an insurer has asked for excessive or unreasonable payments. The department’s computer system is so dysfunctional it can’t issue fines. Until recently, federal examiners relied on decades-old CD-ROM technology to process thousands of reimbursement requests. An effort to hire experts to investigate insurance industry books failed.

The agency also created the opportunity for abuse, the ProPublica investigation found. After lobbying by industry executives, officials loosened the rules for documenting PTSD cases in 2018. The change spurred a wave of questionable claims by workers and suspect payments to insurers, according to industry insiders. Reimbursements to insurance companies more than tripled after the decision, reaching nearly $1 billion through September 2026.

Former Labor officials admit that the agency does not possess the expertise or employees to oversee the money flowing to insurers. “You can’t look under the covers. You just had to pay,” one former senior manager at the agency said.

At issue is a workers’ compensation program for civilians deployed to war zones. In recent conflicts, the U.S. has supplemented its armed forces with hundreds of thousands of workers from across the world to provide security, maintain weapons systems and supply troops with food, housing and transportation. Without them, military officials say, it would be all but impossible for America to go to war.

To protect their workforce, contractors purchase private insurance that the government pays for as part of the bid. When an employee is injured, the insurers cover the cost of medical treatments and lost wages. If a worker dies, they pay benefits to survivors.

But there is a significant exception. If the injury or death is a result of hostilities — as opposed to an ordinary workplace accident like slipping on a wet floor — the U.S. government reimburses the insurance company for the claim. It also adds a handling fee.

Some insurance companies have used this exception to exploit the system in several ways, ProPublica’s investigation found. In many instances, they have settled dubious claims quickly, with little or no investigation, assured that they will receive reimbursement from the government, according to the Labor Department’s internal memo. It’s a churn strategy — cycle cases fast, get paid fast.

Then there’s the opposite tack. Insurers will fight workers in courts for years, racking up expenses as they do so. If they decide to settle the claim, they are able to turn to the Labor Department and report that the injury they sought to deny is in fact authentic. They can then seek reimbursement from the government by asserting that the employee suffered an injury related to hostilities, according to department records. Put bluntly: Insurers change their stories and get paid when they do it.

ProPublica uncovered additional abuses during its investigation, which is based on interviews with scores of current and former federal employees, insurance industry insiders, attorneys for workers and insurers, and civilian employees, along with internal memos, corporate documents and tens of thousands of pages of records obtained through court filings and the Freedom of Information Act.
Do You Have Information on the Defense Base Act or the War Hazards Compensation Act? We’re still reporting. If you know more about this topic, please get in touch.
I am interested in hearing from insiders and whistleblowers — people who know how their organizations work and what is going wrong. I welcome documents and data that deliver concrete evidence.

Contact Me In at least one case, the federal government reimbursed an insurance company for so-called medical expenses that had nothing to do with treating a wounded worker. The insurer received more than $24,000 for “medical” fees that included the cost of hand-delivering records to the insurer’s hired doctor and deposing one of its paid experts. The miscategorization — approved by the Labor Department — allowed the insurer to also collect handling fees on those expenses, adding another $25,000 that it was not entitled to receive, according to department regulations.

Since 2014, four large insurance companies have benefited the most from the system. American International Group, or AIG, has received more than $1 billion, CNA Financial Corp. more than $740 million, Starr insurance more than $730 million and Allied World more than $350 million, according to a ProPublica analysis based on Labor Department records. None of the companies has been accused of wrongdoing.

title_en: Spacecraft reaches Mercury on second-ever mission to enter its orbit
excerpt_en: BepiColombo double probe will map planet’s surface and study its interior to shed light on its unusually large core
body_en: After a voyage of more than eight years and 6bn miles, a joint European-Japanese space mission has arrived at Mercury and is preparing to swing into orbit around the tiny, barely explored world.

The BepiColombo mission will become only the second in history to circle the first rock from the sun and the smallest planet in the solar system when flight controllers fire the spacecraft’s thrusters on Saturday and send it into orbit.

For researchers, the €1.6bn (£1.4bn) mission is the best hope yet of understanding how Mercury formed so close to the sun, why it has a magnetic field, and what makes up the frozen ice that lurks in the planet’s permanently shadowed craters.
“We’re very excited, it’s been a long wait,” said Prof Emma Bunce at the University of Leicester, who has worked on the project for 20 years.

Getting to Mercury poses unusual difficulties. Because the planet is near the centre of the solar system, spacecraft accelerate under the sun’s gravity and must spend much of their time braking to avoid shooting straight past. “It’s a very complex and challenging mission,” said Bunce, the principal investigator on an instrument called the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer, or MIXS, which will analyse the geochemical composition of the planet’s surface.

It will be some months before scientists can start observing Mercury. In early December, the spacecraft will separate into two orbiters, one European, the other Japanese, which will manoeuvre to different polar orbits around the planet. Science operations are due to start in April next year.

The European probe, named the Mercury Planetary Orbiter or MPO, will map the planet’s surface and composition at high resolution, and study Mercury’s interior to shed light on its unusually large core. Its Japanese partner will measure the planet’s magnetic field and its sodium exosphere, the extremely thin layer of gas and atoms that surrounds the planet. Mercury is only 50% larger than the moon but has four times its mass. One question the mission will explore is why the rock is so dense.

Prof Geraint Jones, the lead project scientist on BepiColombo at the European Space Agency, said anticipation of the scientific results had kept everyone enthused during the spacecraft’s eight-year journey.
“We’re expecting to learn a huge amount, bringing more powerful instruments on two spacecraft to study all aspects of the planet – its interior, surface, and the space around it,” he said.

Mercury is a planet of extremes. The tiny world takes 58 Earth days to rotate on its axis, meaning any given spot on the surface can experience daylight for three months and then night-time for three months. It is little more than a third of Earth’s distance from the sun, at only 36m miles. In the day, ground temperatures reach 450C while at night they drop to -180C.

Jones said: “As well as cameras covering a wide range of wavelengths to study the surface, we’ll be ‘tasting’ the gases around the planet, sensing the magnetic field, probing the interior with ultrasensitive instruments, and mapping the shape of the whole planet with a laser.”

The spacecraft are expected to orbit Mercury for about three years, after which they will run out of fuel, lose altitude and ultimately slam into the surface. “Sadly, they are not coming back,” said Bunce.

title_en: Corpus Christi Started Pumping Groundwater at “Lightning Speed.” Rural Residents Fear the Consequences.
excerpt_en: The post Corpus Christi Started Pumping Groundwater at “Lightning Speed.” Rural Residents Fear the Consequences. appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Corpus Christi’s Western Well Field Brenda Bazán for ProPublica and The Texas Tribune Late in 2024, Corpus Christi, Texas, was desperate for water after years of drought. So city officials hatched a plan to tap millions of gallons of water a day from an aquifer that serves dozens of counties across the Texas Gulf Coast.
The city would drill wells — lots of them.

Corpus Christi’s drilling frenzy alarmed rural residents, who worried it threatened their access to water. They mobilized to create a groundwater conservation district that would regulate drilling and, they hoped, limit how much water the city could pump.

Then Corpus Christi officials came up with a peculiar idea. Fearing the residents’ effort could hamper the city’s ambitious plans to tap significant amounts of groundwater, officials asked a local entity to serve as its well regulator.
The advantages: City Council members appoint that entity’s board of directors, and its staff is made up entirely of city employees.

Since that decision last fall, the entity — called the Corpus Christi Aquifer Storage and Recovery Conservation District — has greenlit every city request to drill more wells. In doing so, The Texas Tribune and KRIS 6 found, it fast-tracked its permitting process for the city and overlooked steps that would have slowed down the process for approving the permits — safeguards its own rules require to protect other well users.

A city-commissioned study released this summer found that the drilling plan could cause land around the wells to sink and water levels in other nearby wells to drop significantly. But by then, the district had already approved permits allowing the city to pump up to about 40 million gallons a day from 20 wells, although the city draws less than a third of that daily on average.

The city defended the approvals. It said the district’s rules let the board decide when it has enough information to sign off on a permit and that before it does so, the city gives estimates of how pumping could affect water levels.

But water experts warn that the amount the city is allowed to pump in such a small area is exorbitant. “It’s absolutely unfathomable,” said Drew Molly, the former chief operating officer of Corpus Christi’s water department.
Molly, who is now chief water officer at Houston’s water department, said the district’s “lightning speed” approval of the city’s permits will cause ripple effects locally and across the state.

A water well for pumping groundwater from underground aquifers Brenda Bazán for ProPublica and The Texas Tribune In Texas, fights over limited groundwater supplies will likely intensify as the population booms. Groundwater comes from aquifers and makes up more than half of the state’s water supply.

Aquifers stretch underground across counties and, sometimes, across states. The aquifer Corpus Christi draws from serves dozens of communities along the Gulf of Mexico, including some in Louisiana. Overpumping from aquifers is a key concern in Texas because they need rain and time to refill. As droughts get longer, the state’s water plan shows larger drops in groundwater’s availability compared with other sources.
Groundwater pumping must be approached with caution, experts say. In worst-case scenarios, excessive pumping “can wipe an aquifer out,” said Jarrod Reynolds, a groundwater resource engineer.
“It can be a stopgap, it can be a supplement, but it’s something that’s got to be managed,” Reynolds said.

Corpus Christi’s rapid expansion of groundwater wells offers a critical, if not extreme, example of the challenges presented by a patchwork system for regulating the water that cities, businesses and citizens can extract from the ground.

The coastal city of more than 300,000 residents nearly reached a crisis point earlier this year after persistent drought and years of inaction. It was months away from being unable to meet water demand and faced harsh restrictions to conserve supplies.

Drilling for groundwater became an important fix. So when the possibility of tougher regulation loomed in the wake of the rural residents’ efforts, city officials turned to Corpus Christi’s storage and recovery district, an entity created two decades earlier with the power to approve well permits.

The storage and recovery district is one of nearly 100 such groundwater districts in the state, but it’s the only one with City Council-appointed leaders. Most groundwater districts are led by leaders who are either elected or appointed by county officials — an important distinction since counties are not water suppliers, so there is less concern about any conflict of interest.
Corpus Christi leaders insisted in a written statement that the close ties the city shares with its well regulator will not hamstring efforts to protect the aquifer.

“There is no conflict of interest. City employees involved with the District have no personal or financial interest in permitting decisions,” said Ashley Marion, strategic business manager for the city water department, in the written statement. She added that, “The City and District share an interest in protecting and sustainably managing regional groundwater.”
Marion also said the city tracks water levels and physical conditions at the wells and adjusts pumping rates based on daily data and long-term modeling.
But the arrangement has drawn concern from water experts across the state, an outgoing state lawmaker and at least one of the storage and recovery district’s own board members.

title_en: Anthropic shares end first day of trading at $97 as Wall Street closes sharply lower – as it happened
excerpt_en: All ⁠three major US stock indexes ⁠ended the session sharply lower after record-breaking IPO by maker behind AI agent Claude
body_en: Democratic US senator Adam Schiff has penned an op-ed in the Wall Street Journal warning about “the systemic risk to the economy” posed by the AI industry – and demanding that Congress rule out a taxpayer-funded bailout should the sector collapse.
Highlighting the turmoil surrounding Nvidia since the spectacular exit of its CEO Jensen Huang, Schiff writes:

This technology [artificial intelligence] has boundless potential to enhance our lives and expand our individual and collective capacity. But as the turmoil around Nvidia reminds us, this swift and massive investment also carries significant risk that an industry downturn or a bubble could destabilize the American economy. In the first six days of the scandal involving Nvidia and its former CEO, the sector lost $500bn in value.

Given the risks to our economy and investors, Congress must make sure that industry understands this: No company is too big to fail, and in the event of a financial collapse of the tech sector, there will be no taxpayer-funded bailout.

The AI industry, after less than five years of market power, is already estimated to represent 3.6% of our nation’s economy. But much of its explosive build-out is financed by an opaque debt structure and expectations of increasing profitability. This may be the biggest economic gamble in American history, and policymakers should make clear that Congress and American taxpayers won’t act as its fail-safe should this industry falter under its own immense weight.

Schiff goes on to remind the reader: “We have seen this movie before.” Invoking the bank bailout of 2008, he writes: “ If these enormous bets fail, Big Tech and Wall Street billionaires will no doubt turn to Washington for emergency rescue, a path unfortunately well-trodden by corporate giants before them. But the risk should be borne by these companies and their investors, not working families.”

The billionaire investors may be taking this gamble with the assumption that as in 2008, they will be bailed out for failed investments and corporate risk-taking. Congressional majorities should be clear: We won’t bail them out.
Anthropic has made a blockbuster stock market debut – shattering already high expectations.
The AP has put together some numbers to help you understand Thursday’s IPO:

The amount in proceeds raised by the offering: $81bn. That makes Anthropic’s debut the biggest ever. Ahead of Thursday’s trading, it offered 980m shares priced at $83 each, putting Anthropic ahead of Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which set a previous record with its IPO proceeds of about $75bn in June.

Anthropic’s initial valuation: $1.5tn. The initial price per share was set at $83. But that spiked more than 30% to open at $111.50 a share — pushing the company’s total valuation by half a trillion dollars to $2.01tn just before noon ET.

By market close Thursday, Anthropic finished its first trading day at $97.17 per share. That’s still over 17% higher than its initial public offering price, and amounts to a market value of roughly $1.75tn. In June, SpaceX ended its first day of trading on the public market with a valuation of $2.1tn. Its market cap has since fallen to closer to $1.95tn.
Number of public companies that have reached the trillion-dollar club in the S+P 500: 11

Apple currently leads the pack at $5.1tn, followed by Microsoft ($3.8tn) and Nvidia ($3.6tn), among others. That does not count SpaceX and Anthropic, which also have joined the trillion-dollar club even though they aren’t in the S+P 500 index yet. Only in recent memory have major corporations been valued over $1tn. iPhone maker Apple was the first to pass that threshold, back in 2018.
There are more than 8.2 billion people living on Earth today, per the US Census Bureau. If $1tn was divided among the entire population, each person would receive almost $122.

Summary Anthropic shares closed about 17% higher on their first day of trading on Thursday, despite investor fears of a possible AI bubble and public anxiety over the technology. The shares ended the session at around $97, up from a record-breaking IPO price of $83, after opening at $111.50 and briefly valuing the creator of the Claude chatbot at about $2tn – making the AI giant’s debut the biggest in history. The company’s valuation after the close stands at around $1.3tn, down from the high of $2tn recorded earlier.

However, a 2% slump at the close suggests that Anthropic’s stellar debut wasn’t enough to carry the wider market, which struggled for much of the day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average sank 2.2%, while the S&P 500 fell 2% and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.3%, preliminary data showed. The S&P 500 fell for a sixth straight day - its longest losing streak since 19 April 2024 – amid concerns about the sustainability of the AI boom and after the drama surrounding Nvidia following the fall of its CEO Jensen Huang last week dragged the company’s shares down.

Shortly before ringing the Nasdaq opening bell, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei issued a warning about the dangers of AI but said they weren’t inevitable. “We’ve always been honest that this techology has very real risks … from misuse of the technology by individuals or nation states, to economic disruption, to losing control of AI systems,” he said. “Avoiding them depends on the choices made by the people making AI. There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety, versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety.”

title_en: The Trump DOJ Quietly Intervened to Ink a Huge Payout to a Trump Golf Pro
excerpt_en: The post The Trump DOJ Quietly Intervened to Ink a Huge Payout to a Trump Golf Pro appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: President Donald Trump and his son Eric Trump at the Trump National Doral Golf Club in Florida Joe Raedle/Getty Images Top Trump administration officials intervened to help a longtime golf pro at Trump National Golf Club Hudson Valley secure a half-million-dollar payout from the IRS. A company connected to Trump’s media business also got a half-million.

The deal grew out of a little-noticed federal class-action lawsuit filed in 2025 by five individuals and companies. The group got $2.5 million after accusing the IRS of failing to protect their tax information.

The law permits a $1,000 payment to victims for each instance of an unauthorized inspection or disclosure of tax data. In this case, however, the government’s monetary settlement is 250 times higher than what the law calls for given the allegations. Victims can receive more money if they show actual damages, but multiple officials say such cases almost never result in payments approaching this size. These generous settlements have raised concerns because IRS Office of Chief Counsel attorneys were not consulted about the settlement terms, as is standard practice, according to people familiar with the case and documents seen by ProPublica.

What’s more, those payouts didn’t resolve the lawsuit. After the settlement was made, two more people came forward seeking to continue the litigation — and both are connected to Trump businesses. One is a retired accountant who worked at the same Trump property as the golf pro. The second appears to be a former lifeguard at a different Trump golf club in Westchester County, New York.

Gil Rothenberg, a law professor at American University who ran the appellate section at the Justice Department tax division for 15 years before leaving in 2019, said the deal “is not passing the smell test.”

“It’s not just the amount that I find odd and unusual,” he told ProPublica. “It’s the fact that this settlement amount occurred before any final decision by the district court, and basically the DOJ is giving up any right to appeal.”

The case in question is Safe Harbor International LLC v. Booz Allen Hamilton, Internal Revenue Service and the U.S. Department of the Treasury, brought in Maryland federal court. Plaintiffs claim that the IRS and the government contractor Booz Allen failed to implement proper safeguards and were negligent in allowing Booz Allen employee Charles Littlejohn to steal tax records and give them to news organizations, including ProPublica.

President Donald Trump sued over similar claims earlier this year, seeking $10 billion in damages. In response, then-acting Attorney General Todd Blanche announced a $1.776 billion “anti-weaponization fund” to resolve the case. That settlement was structured to grant the president’s inner circle the authority to green-light payouts of government money to whomever they wanted. The public erupted in outrage. Democratic and even a small number of Republican lawmakers objected to the proposed fund, and the department dropped the idea as Blanche sought Senate confirmation for his position.

Critics fear that the DOJ’s unusual payment in the Safe Harbor case could be a backdoor way to revive something similar to the controversial slush fund. In all, plaintiffs claim the size of the class is “in the tens or hundreds of thousands.” If a significant number of those plaintiffs secured the same payment, the total liability for the federal government could reach into the billions of dollars. A judge has yet to rule on whether to allow the case to proceed.

That group could include other Trump allies and friends. It even “opens the door to Trump himself benefiting from this settlement,” said John Koskinen, who served as IRS commissioner from 2013 to 2017.

Spokespeople for the Justice Department and IRS said they would not comment on a pending case. A White House spokesperson said that the Justice Department is “promoting efficient resolution of cases to avoid extraordinary liability.”

Between 2018 and 2020, Littlejohn, the Booz Allen contractor, leaked confidential IRS data to ProPublica and The New York Times, he has said. The data included years of Trump’s taxes and information on thousands of the wealthiest people in the country.

Do You Have a Justice Department Tip for ProPublica? If you know about this case and the government’s handling of it, please contact our reporting team. I’m grateful for any documents that sources can share. Protecting sources is something I take very seriously.
If you have tips about Big Tech and the Trump administration, please get in touch.

Contact Me ProPublica published stories on the tax-avoidance strategies of the ultrawealthy. The New York Times reported in 2020 on how Trump declared large annual losses to avoid paying taxes. Together, the two news organizations reported that Trump was fighting with the IRS over a long-running audit that could have cost him $100 million.
Littlejohn pleaded guilty in October 2023 to unauthorized disclosure of tax information. A judge sentenced him to five years in prison.

The IRS sent letters to more than 400,000 individuals and businesses to alert them that their taxpayer information had been “inappropriately disclosed” by Littlejohn. As ProPublica has previously stated, we obtained the tax return information of the top 0.001% of individuals by income, a figure in the thousands. Limited information about other entities appears in the records only to the extent that it is related to the group of top earners.
A number of taxpayers who received the notice filed civil lawsuits demanding compensation from the IRS and Booz Allen.

title_en: Jimmy Kimmel on Trump’s meeting with Xi and Putin: ‘I guess Darth Vader couldn’t make it’
excerpt_en: Late-night hosts discussed Trump’s friendly meeting with the Russian and Chinese leaders at the Apec summit
body_en: Late-night hosts mocked Donald Trump ’s friendly meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping as well as the administration’s muddled response to various tech outages.

Jimmy Kimmel Jimmy Kimmel opened Wednesday’s show with footage of Trump’s visit to the Apec summit in Shenzhen, China, where the president “got a rare personal greeting on the tarmac from President Xi”.

Kimmel then played footage of Trump disembarking Air Force One to receive a warm embrace from the Chinese leader. “You know, President Xi doesn’t usually do that sort of thing, but I guess he wanted to see what a $400m bribe from Qatar looks like up close,” the host joked, referring to Trump’s new Air Force One aircraft, a $400m “gift” from Qatar.
“Trump was excited to be reunited with his friend, the Chinese president,” he added. “You know, it’s been a while. He finally has new male buttocks to fixate on.
Related: Jimmy Kimmel on mass outages: ‘The US is running like a McDonald’s soft-serve machine’
“Funny, Trump spent the last 10 years calling Democrats communists,” he quipped. “He gets off the plane, gives a big wet kiss to an actual communist, a real one.
“But he put his best hoof forward,” Kimmel continued, noting that the president “painted his hands real pretty for the event” with obvious putty-like makeup that did not match his skin tone.
“This hand has now been paved over more times than his name at the Kennedy Center,” Kimmel joked. “Either that’s his makeup or he’s eating peanut butter straight out of the jar again.”
Kimmel then played footage of Trump and Xi joined on the red carpet by the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, whom the US president once again referred to as his “friend”.

“I guess Darth Vader couldn’t make it to fill out the foursome,” Kimmel wisecracked. “There you see Trump reunited with the leader of the country that makes his merch, and the leader of the country that made him president.

“You can tell Trump feels jealous when he meets with Xi and Putin and sees all the cool dictator stuff they get to do,” he added. “It’s like when you’re a kid and you visit your cousin who had Sega Genesis.”

Seth Meyers And on Late Night, Seth Meyers reacted to the recent cascade of tech outages. “I don’t know if you guys have noticed this lately, but it feels like things are breaking. And by things, I mean all the things,” he said before listing technical failures at Microsoft, major US banks, Apple, American air traffic control systems and the National Security Agency all in the last week. The causes have been vague; JP Morgan Chase, for one, attributed their outage to “technical issues”.

“Oh, is it a ‘technical issue’?” Meyers deadpanned. “The problems we’re having with the internet and routers and AI aren’t caused by Mercury in retrograde or someone made a badly worded wish on the novelty toy from Obsession.”

But not to fret – the homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, was on the case, appearing this week on Fox News to reassure the public that “the homeland is secure. Our banking system is secure. And when something like this happens, we’re able to react, and react fast. You see what happened Friday night with the FAA.”
“Yeah, we did. That sucked!” Meyers responded. “The nation’s air traffic control system broke down because of a router somewhere in Arkansas?”

In the same interview, Mullin tried to reassure viewers that he spoke to one anonymous “guy that’s very smart with tech”, who explained that AI – or “SI”, to use the preferred parlance of the Trump administration – “self-fixes itself. As it starts self-fixing itself, it’s like doing a change order on house. When you do a change order on a house, everything else starts changing and it’s a ripple effect.” That long explanation “kinda made sense to me”, he added.

“Does it? Because it makes no fucking sense to me,” Meyers said. “You sound like a gym teacher subbing in for health class – ‘OK team, listen up, when the egg comes down and self-fixes itself with the sperm, think of it like a running back carrying the ball through the gap, and you know there’s a ripple effect.’”

title_en: Fossil fuel lobbyists are trying to derail climate action once again at COP31. Can they be stopped?
excerpt_en: The whole point of this summit is to address climate change. Why are fossil fuel cheerleaders still allowed in the door?
body_en: Burak Kara/Getty This week, it was revealed that 100 corporations and industry groups tied to fossil fuel interests – including the US multinational ExxonMobil and French energy company TotalEnergies – have sent delegations to this year’s global climate summit COP31 in Turkey.

These climate talks have a long history of lobbyist interference. More than 1,600 fossil fuel lobbyists attended the COP30 talks in Brazil last year, and more than 1,700 at the 2024 talks in Azerbaijan.

This is a problem. The whole point of these long-running United Nations negotiations is to address human-caused climate change, which is primarily driven by burning oil, gas and coal – the very products these lobbyists are paid to promote.
At COP31, fossil lobbyists will have been hard at work promoting fossil fuels. Their methods often draw on what academics call “ discourses of delay ”.

This is how it works. To slow the shift away from fossil fuels, lobbyists spread disinformation, such as claiming fossil fuels are part of the solution (“gas is a transition fuel”), that future technologies will save us (carbon capture), or we’re doomed and it’s too late to act. Oil and gas companies have dramatically increased their Google ads in the month leading up to COP31, for example.

Researchers have shown fossil fuel lobbyists use a two-pronged strategy. First, they point to a lack of international action as a reason for not acting on climate change at home. Second, they work to stymie progress at the same international talks.
A new UN report says it’s now too late to hold the global temperature rise to 1.5°C. The world will likely pass this threshold in 2030.
A big reason for this is obstruction by lobbyists of climate policies that target the root cause of climate change – fossil fuels.
So, why are fossil fuel lobbyists allowed into these talks?
Pushback in Brazil At last year’s COP30 summit, host country Brazil tried to push back against fossil fuel lobbyists.
Alongside the UN and UNESCO, Brazil launched an international partnership to counter climate change disinformation and misinformation.
Thirty countries have since signed onto the declaration, which calls out the:

growing impact of disinformation, misinformation, denialism […] and other tactics used to undermine the integrity of information on climate change, which diminish public understanding, delay urgent action, and threaten the global climate response and societal stability.
Lobbyists gain access to the talks in different ways, including through affiliations with non-governmental organisations and industry groups and as part of official government delegations.

While this year’s draft negotiating text makes reference to information integrity, there’s still no clear code of conduct or meaningful disclosure of fossil fuel industry ties for the thousands of delegates attending COP31. There are no clear, explicit rules against spreading climate disinformation.

COP30 President Andre Correa do Lago (centre) listens to his advisers at the conference in Brazil last year. Brazil has since produced a global roadmap for transitioning away from fossil fuels. Pablo Porciuncula/Getty A long history of lobbying Sadly, this story is all too familiar. For as long as there have been international climate talks, fossil fuel lobbyists have tried to persuade countries not to act with the urgency the science demands.

It took more than a quarter of a century of climate talks before fossil fuels were explicitly addressed at the Glasgow COP in 2021. Until then, the focus was on greenhouse gas emissions – but not the fossil fuels causing them.
Corporate fossil fuel lobbyists have been assisted by so-called petrostates, such as Russia and Saudi Arabia, whose economies are highly dependent on oil and gas production.
And when the oil- and gas-producing states Azerbaijan and the United Arab Emirates hosted the COP talks in 2023 and 2024, respectively, both countries used the summit to push new fossil fuel deals.
What are lobbyists targeting this time? There are more than 100 different agenda items up for debate at COP31, many of which are opposed by fossil fuel lobbyists.
Negotiators are still discussing a UN initiative designed to rapidly increase efforts to cut greenhouse gas emissions, for instance.

Alongside the official agenda, COP President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum released a separate “action” agenda organised around ten themes. Some of these, such as transitioning to clean energy, threaten fossil fuel interests.
